data.hypothesis: Compared with the measured full-state cache (0.1790 s) and the x/y-cache hybrid without shared z state (0.2878 s), this variant tests whether a compact x/y smooth-weight-only cache plus shared per-octave z state can limit scratch traffic. It deliberately recomputes x/y lattice cells and fractions, so extra preprocessing may erase the saved weight work; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: Per-axis state reuse should be evaluated end-to-end, including allocation and state access; isolated arithmetic savings do not establish a benefit.
memory_lessons.claim: The measured full x/y plus z state candidate was correct and faster than the baseline (0.1790 s versus 0.3109 s), while the x/y full-state hybrid without shared z was 0.2878 s. The lattice/fraction-only variant was correct but slower and noisy at 0.3813 s.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this distinct x/y-weight-only plus shared-z layout at the fixed tolerance on n=768 and smaller or shifted bounds, keeping it separate from the full-state and no-z hybrids.

data.notes: This is a distinct hybrid layout: only x/y smooth weights are retained per axis and octave; x/y cells and fractions are recomputed, while z cell, offset, and smooth weight are shared. The vector allocation and all cache population/access are inside noise_serial. Preserve the candidate separately and await controller correctness and timing, including smaller and shifted inputs.
transformations: Add per-axis, per-octave smooth-weight arrays for x and y, using the original coordinate expression order before scaling by lambda.
Recompute x/y lattice cells and fractions for each pixel and octave instead of storing them; reuse precomputed z cell, offset, and smooth weight for each octave.

Retain the original gradient ordering, interpolation ordering, per-pixel accumulation, lambda progression, and amplitude progression; perform all allocations and state access within noise_serial timing.
